paper_did: It subjected the equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high‐entropy alloy to severe plastic deformation through swaging followed by quasi‐static compression, dynamic uniaxial compression, and dynamic shear tests (using a forced hat‐shaped geometry), including experiments at cryogenic temperatures (77 K).

It introduced a high density of defects (dislocations, stacking faults, twins, and hcp transformation) via controlled mechanical processing and characterized the resulting microstructure using EBSD, TEM (with high‐resolution imaging and FFT analysis), and energy‐dispersive spectroscopy.

It measured the macroscopic mechanical response (stress–strain curves across different strain rates) and provided a free‐energy–based argument (using stacking‐fault energy calculations and critical dislocation density estimates) to rationalize the progression from dislocation plasticity to twinning, phase transformation (fcc to hcp), and ultimately amorphization.
paper_reported: It reported that under extreme deformation the CrMnFeCoNi alloy develops a complex microstructure featuring a high density of dislocations, stacking faults, and twins, along with an fcc-to-hcp phase transformation and the formation of nanoscale amorphous regions (islands and bands) at the intersections of deformation packets.

It demonstrated that amorphization occurs via a solid‐state process under both quasi‐static and dynamic conditions—with the dynamic (high strain rate) and cryogenic tests promoting a higher preponderance of amorphous features—thus adding an extra deformation mechanism that improves toughness.

It showed that the absorbed deviatoric strain energy in predeformed materials nearly doubles relative to the annealed alloy, suggesting that the interplay of crystalline defects and amorphous phase formation contributes to enhanced impact resistance.
paper_proposed: It proposed that by tailoring the alloy composition (for instance, lowering the stacking‐fault energy further) and optimizing thermal–mechanical processing (to introduce a higher density of defects), one could maximize the beneficial effects of defect‐mediated amorphization and develop superior alloys for extreme loading environments.

It also suggested that systematic, displacement‐controlled experiments (despite their experimental challenges, especially under dynamic testing) are needed to quantitatively relate the accumulation of defects with the evolving volume fraction of amorphous material.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Variations in chemical short‐range order (CSRO) induced by complete versus reduced elemental complexity modulate the local stacking‐fault energy distribution, thereby altering defect accumulation and the onset of amorphization during deformation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Thermomechanically processed, single‐phase FCC equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni (quinary) alloy and its equiatomic quaternary/ternary subsets with similar grain size and defect density pre-deformation.
hypotheses.intervention: Perform controlled quasi‐static deformation tests while using atom probe tomography (APT) and high-resolution TEM to measure CSRO and local stacking-fault configurations at regions of deformation-induced defects.
hypotheses.conditions: Experiments at ambient temperature with identical pre-deformation histories and strain rates ensuring similar macroscopic deformation conditions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Localized regions with distinct chemical short-range order that affect the local stacking-fault energy and defect accumulation.
hypotheses.mechanism: The full quinary alloy, due to the presence of all five elements, develops a more uniform and possibly stronger CSRO, which broadens the distribution of local stacking fault energies. This variation increases the free-energy barrier needed for defect coalescence into amorphous zones. In contrast, removal of one or two constituents in quaternary/ternary alloys reduces CSRO complexity, leading to a narrower stacking-fault energy distribution and lowering the effective barrier to amorphous region nucleation. This shift in microstructural evolution leads to differences in work hardening and failure behavior.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary/ternary alloys will exhibit earlier onset of amorphous island formation and a higher volumetric fraction of amorphous regions at the same strain—potentially a shift by tens of percent in the strain at which amorphization becomes noticeable. This should correlate with a less gradual work-hardening curve.
hypotheses.baseline: The mechanical behavior and defect accumulation pathways observed in the fully equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy as documented in PMC7846165.
hypotheses.boundary: Applies under quasi-static deformation at ambient temperature in single-phase FCC alloys with similar grain structures and pre-deformation defect densities.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Quantitative relationship between CSRO variation and local stacking fault energy distribution is not well established prior to testing.

hypotheses.mechanism: In the full quinary alloy, the complete set of solutes can partition favorably to twin and dislocation interfaces during deformation, effectively pinning these boundaries and retarding the coalescence of defects into amorphous shear bands. Consequently, twin boundaries may become less stable, leading to earlier accumulation of local strain and more rapid amorphous transformation. This difference in twin boundary stabilization directly influences work-hardening behavior and failure modes.

paper_did: Fabricated equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 single‐phase and non‐equiatomic Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14 dual‐phase high‐entropy alloys by arc melting, homogenization, rolling, and annealing.
Performed quasi‐static tensile tests at temperatures ranging from 25°C to 800°C with identical preheat and strain rate conditions.
Characterized the microstructure and local chemistry using SEM, TEM, XRD, and especially atom probe tomography (APT) to detect nanoscale segregation at grain boundaries.
Implemented a grain boundary (GB) segregation engineering strategy by introducing pre‐existing Cr‐rich secondary (σ) phases to absorb embrittling elements and mitigate ductility loss.
paper_reported: Demonstrated that the single‐phase Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 alloy suffers ductility loss at intermediate temperatures (400–800°C) correlated with intergranular cracking.
Revealed by APT that fast nanoclustering/segregation of principal elements (Cr, Ni, and Mn) at GBs reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation.
Showed that preexisting Cr‐rich σ phases in the dual‐phase Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14 alloy can ‘absorb’ embrittling elements, resulting in improved ductility at intermediate temperatures.
paper_proposed: Proposed a GB segregation engineering strategy to deliberately shift the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting embrittling element–rich secondary phases.
Suggested that tailoring the morphology, size, and distribution of secondary phases may further enhance ductility and optimize the strength–ductility–temperature relations in HEAs.
Implied that the nanoclustering-induced GB decohesion mechanism may be a common phenomenon across HEAs, guiding future alloy design.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Elastic heterogeneity due to chemical complexity leads to localized strain concentrations in the quinary alloy that promote early fracture along critical interfaces.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni single-phase FCC alloy with a homogeneous microstructure after standardized thermo‐mechanical processing, compared with its equiatomic quaternary and ternary FCC subsets.
hypotheses.intervention: Perform a controlled comparison by preparing tensile specimens of the quinary alloy versus its quaternary and ternary subsets under the same thermomechanical history and testing them at intermediate temperatures (400–800°C) while mapping local strain fields at the micron to submicron scale (e.g., using high-resolution digital image correlation or synchrotron diffraction).
hypotheses.conditions: Tensile tests at a strain rate of ~10^–3 s^–1, specimen preheat hold (~10 min) at intermediate temperatures, identical processing history for all compositions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Nanometer-scale elastic modulus fluctuations and chemical inhomogeneities in the matrix that lead to uneven load distribution across grains and grain boundaries.
hypotheses.mechanism: The presence of five distinct elements in the quinary alloy increases atomic-level variations in bonding and modulus, creating local regions with lower stiffness. Under deformation, these elastic heterogeneities concentrate strain, thereby accelerating crack initiation at interfaces compared to the more uniform quaternary or ternary alloys.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The quinary alloy is expected to show earlier local strain localization and a lower uniform elongation compared to its lower-component counterparts; the effect magnitude may be moderate to large if the elastic modulus variation is significant.
hypotheses.baseline: Mechanical response of the equiatomic quinary alloy as previously characterized after similar processing.
hypotheses.boundary: Applies during intermediate temperature tensile deformation where diffusion and dislocation activity are active but segregation effects are not dominated by precipitate formation (roughly 400–800°C).
hypotheses.uncertainty: The quantitative degree of modulus variation and its strain localization effect may be sensitive to minor processing variations and measurement resolution.

hypotheses.structural_mediator: Dislocation slip and deformation twinning networks within the FCC matrix.
hypotheses.mechanism: The full complement of five elements in the quinary alloy is expected to lower the intrinsic stacking fault energy more markedly than in quaternary/ternary counterparts. A lower SFE facilitates the nucleation of deformation twins, which, while initially enhancing strain hardening, can lead to strain localization and early crack initiation due to twin boundary embrittlement and incompatibility in plastic flow.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The quinary alloy should display a higher density of deformation twins, an earlier onset of rapid strain hardening, and reduced ductility compared to the lower-component alloys. The effect is predicted to be moderate in scale, though the precise decrease in ductility remains uncertain before experimental determination.

hypotheses.uncertainty: Quantitative SFE differences and the extent to which these drive twinning rather than other mechanisms (like dislocation slip) remain to be precisely measured in these alloys.

paper_did: Synthesized equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with a single-phase FCC structure and an average grain size around 50 μm, and also fabricated a dual-phase Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14 HEA with preexisting Cr‐rich σ phases.

Performed quasi‐static tensile tests over a range of temperatures (25°C to 800°C) with a constant strain rate of 10^–3 s^–1, including a pretest temperature hold (~10 min) to simulate intermediate-temperature deformation.

Carried out detailed microstructural and chemical characterizations using SEM, TEM, and atom probe tomography (APT) to reveal that, during tensile tests at intermediate temperatures (around 700°C), nanosegregation (nanoclustering) of the principal elements Cr, Ni, and Mn occurs at grain boundaries and correlates with intergranular cracking and ductility loss.
paper_reported: The single‐phase equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA shows dramatic ductility loss at intermediate temperatures (400°C to 700°C), which is correlated with the formation of nanoclusters of Cr, Ni, and Mn at grain boundaries that reduce GB cohesion and promote crack initiation.

APT analyses demonstrated that the embrittled GBs are enriched with the principal elements (Cr, Ni, and Mn) while no secondary phase (intermetallic precipitates) was detected during the short high-temperature tensile tests.

A grain boundary (GB) segregation engineering strategy was successfully demonstrated by preintroducing Cr‐rich σ phases (in the Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14 HEA), which absorb the embrittling elements away from GBs, thereby effectively mitigating the ductility loss at intermediate temperatures.
paper_proposed: The paper proposes that GB segregation engineering—namely, shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from the GBs into preexisting embrittling element–enriched secondary phases—can be a viable strategy to tailor the strength–ductility–temperature relations in HEAs.
It suggests that further optimization of the morphology, size, and distribution of these precipitates could lead to improved ductility at intermediate temperatures.

paper_did: Designed and fabricated a VCrMnFeCoNi high‐entropy alloy (10V15Cr5Mn35Fe10Co25Ni) using thermodynamic calculations and controlled thermomechanical processing.

Employed homogenization, cold rolling, and annealing at 750 °C (for partial recrystallization) and 900 °C (for full recrystallization) to produce distinct microstructures (coarse non‐recrystallized grains with retained twins versus fine recrystallized grains).

Characterized the microstructures using X‐ray diffraction, EBSD, and TEM to document deformation twins formed during room‐temperature processing and additional twin formation under cryogenic tensile loading.

Tested mechanical properties at room and cryogenic (−196 °C) temperatures, demonstrating that the partially recrystallized (H750) alloy exhibited ultra‐high yield and tensile strengths (yield ≈970 MPa and tensile ≈1314 MPa) with substantial ductility.
paper_reported: The cryogenic tensile strength and ductility improvements are linked to the combined action of room‐temperature deformation twins (retained in coarse, non‐recrystallized grains) and additional twin formation during tensile testing.
Grain size plays a decisive role in controlling the critical stress for twinning; coarse grains promote twinning while fine recrystallized grains (in the H900 alloy) show few twins.

Retained deformation twins in the non‐recrystallized regions act as strong barriers to dislocation motion, thereby enhancing the yield strength and contributing to the unique combination of strength and ductility.
paper_proposed: Exploiting non‐recrystallized grains and the associated retained deformation twins as a design concept to achieve ultra‐high strength in high‐entropy alloys.
Utilizing room‐temperature deformation twinning through precise thermomechanical treatments as a means to tailor cryogenic mechanical performance in HEAs.
Encouraging future work aimed at optimizing the balance between recrystallized and non‐recrystallized regions to further enhance mechanical properties at extreme service temperatures.

paper_did: Designed a new non‐equi‐atomic 10V15Cr5Mn35Fe10Co25Ni high‐entropy alloy using computational thermodynamic methods.

Processed the alloy by homogenization, room‐temperature cold rolling (without hot‐rolling induced grain refinement), and subsequent annealing at 750 °C (partial recrystallization, H750 alloy) or 900 °C (full recrystallization, H900 alloy).

Characterized the phase (single FCC), microstructures (grain sizes, retained deformation twins in non‐recrystallized grains), and mechanical properties (tensile tests at room and cryogenic temperatures) using XRD, EBSD, TEM, KAM mapping, and mechanical testing.
paper_reported: The partially recrystallized H750 alloy exhibits a dual microstructure of fine recrystallized grains and coarse non‐recrystallized grains that retain deformation twins from cold rolling.

These retained twins, along with additional twinning during cryogenic tensile deformation, lead to ultra‐high yield strengths (~970 MPa at cryogenic temperatures) and tensile strengths (~1,314 MPa) while still maintaining good ductility.
The study established that controlled usage of non‐recrystallized grains with room‐temperature deformation twins can be an effective strengthening mechanism in high‐entropy alloys.
paper_proposed: That room‐temperature deformation twinning coupled with partial recrystallization (i.e., retaining non‐recrystallized grains) can be exploited as a practical method to achieve ultra‐high strength in HEAs, particularly at cryogenic temperatures.
That such thermomechanical processing—eschewing grain refinement by hot rolling—offers a promising design concept for next‐generation ultra‐high‐strength and ductile HEAs.

paper_did: Fabricated equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high‐entropy alloy specimens by arc-melting, drop-casting, cold-rolling, and recrystallization to obtain single-phase FCC microstructures with controlled grain sizes (≈8, 70, and 340 μm).

Machined single-crystal micropillars using focused ion beam (FIB) from selected grains and conducted compression tests at room temperature (and 77 K for bulk specimens) to study size effects on critical resolved shear stress (CRSS).

Measured mechanical properties including CRSS (showing an inverse power-law scaling with an exponent of −0.63 and a bulk CRSS of ~33–43 MPa), elastic moduli, Hall-Petch behavior, and dislocation characteristics (planar slip, dissociation into Shockley partials with measured separations leading to a stacking fault energy of ~30 ± 5 mJ/m²) via TEM and other techniques.
paper_reported: A robust size effect in CRSS where micropillar tests yield an inverse power-law behavior (exponent −0.63) independent of crystal orientation, and extrapolation gives a bulk CRSS (~33–43 MPa) significantly higher than that of pure FCC metals.

Dislocation investigations revealed that perfect dislocations dissociate into Shockley partials with separations (≈3.5–4.5 nm for screw and 5–8 nm for edge orientations) that, when combined with a relatively high shear modulus, result in a stacking fault energy of ~30 ± 5 mJ/m².

Comparisons with binary FCC solid-solution alloys using Fleischer and Labusch models indicate that the observed CRSS is in the expected range for alloys with high solute concentrations and atomic size misfits, while the Hall-Petch relation and temperature-dependent yield behavior were also characterized.
paper_proposed: The paper hints at future work involving the growth and comprehensive compression testing of bulk single crystals to further validate the extrapolated bulk CRSS values.
It also identifies the need for additional studies to clarify factors such as impurity effects and to more rigorously quantify the solid-solution hardening mechanisms in these high-entropy alloys.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Variations in stacking fault energy (SFE) induced by differing elemental interactions in the quinary versus the quaternary and ternary alloys alter the dislocation dissociation and cross-slip behavior, thereby affecting the strain-hardening behavior and failure modes.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni (quinary) alloy and its corresponding quaternary/ternary subsets, all in a single-phase FCC state after controlled thermomechanical processing.
hypotheses.intervention: Synthesize compositions with one or more elements systematically removed (to form quaternary and ternary subsets) while ensuring identical processing; measure their stacking fault energies (via TEM analysis of Shockley partial separation) and perform mechanical deformation tests (micropillar compression or low-temperature deformation tests).
hypotheses.conditions: Experiments conducted at room temperature and at cryogenic temperatures (e.g., 77 K) to probe temperature-dependent changes in SFE-related deformation mechanisms.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The dissociation width of dislocations (i.e., separation between Shockley partials) and the ease of cross-slip as mediated by the effective SFE.
hypotheses.mechanism: In the quinary alloy, the complex interplay of elemental interactions results in an SFE (measured ~30 ± 5 mJ/m²) that controls the extent of dissociation of dislocations into partials. Removing one or more elements (forming quaternary/ternary alloys) alters the balance of atomic interactions and may lead to a shift in the SFE. A lower SFE will further increase the partial separation, inhibiting cross-slip and potentially promoting deformation twinning, while a higher SFE will facilitate cross-slip and alter strain hardening behavior. This variation in SFE, even if modest, changes the operative deformation mechanisms and thus the macroscopic mechanical properties.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to the quinary alloy, a quaternary or ternary alloy with a reduced SFE would be expected to show larger partial dislocation separations, reduced cross-slip, enhanced planar slip or even increased twinning activity, resulting in higher strain-hardening rates and possibly different failure modes (such as earlier onset of twinning-induced plasticity). Conversely, if the alloy’s SFE increases upon reducing constituent count, easier cross-slip may lower yield strength. Mechanical test data (stress-strain curves) and TEM measurement of partial separation distances should reveal these trends.
hypotheses.baseline: The quinary alloy baseline as given in the paper [PMC5075899::web::abstract, discussion] with an SFE ~30 ± 5 mJ/m² and known dislocation dissociation behavior.
hypotheses.boundary: Hypothesis is applicable only when all alloys remain single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing and are tested under comparable conditions.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The magnitude of SFE change due to compositional variation may be modest, and the quantitative linking of SFE shifts to macroscopic mechanical properties requires careful interpretation; exact values might have higher uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys with the same thermomechanical history. Use TEM to measure Shockley partial separation distances (as a proxy for SFE) and measure macroscopic deformation behavior using micropillar compression or bulk tests at room and cryogenic temperatures. Compare strain-hardening rates and twinning activity.

pool.label: C1
pool.builds_on: The finding that CrCoNi shows a robust fcc-to-hcp transformation due to a lower energy difference, a mechanism that is suppressed in the quinary alloy by magnetic frustration from Mn (PMC5893566::web::000, PMC5893566::web::003, PMC5893566::web::007).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a controlled compositional modification (reduced Mn content) in the quinary alloy to reinstate the deformation-triggered phase transformation mechanism and strengthen the alloy—an approach not attempted or proposed in the original paper.

fields.hypothesis: Reducing the Mn content in the CrMnFeCoNi quinary alloy will restore a stronger driving force for the deformation-induced fcc-to-hcp transformation, thereby enhancing work hardening and strength relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi (quinary alloy) that is single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing.
fields.intervention: Prepare alloys with a controlled reduction of Mn (with corresponding slight increase in the relative concentrations of the other four elements) while maintaining a single-phase FCC structure.
fields.conditions: Same thermomechanical processing conditions (deformation to high strain, e.g. ≈55% true strain, ambient to cryogenic temperatures as in the paper) applied to both the baseline and Mn-reduced alloy.
fields.structural_mediator: Increased formation of localized nano-hcp laths at stacking faults and twin boundaries.
fields.mechanism: In CrCoNi, a clear fcc-to-hcp transformation is driven by a lower energy state of hcp relative to fcc (with dislocation activity triggering the transformation), whereas in the quinary CrMnFeCoNi the presence of Mn induces magnetic frustration that reduces the energy difference between the phases. Reducing the Mn content will mitigate magnetic frustration, thereby re-establishing a chemical and magnetic environment favorable for hcp nucleation at defect sites. This additional barrier to dislocation glide enhances strain hardening and strength.
fields.predicted_outcome: The Mn-reduced alloy will exhibit a measurable increase in the density and thickness of deformation-induced hcp regions (observed via TEM/HAADF-STEM) and a higher work hardening rate along with increased yield strength (directionally improved by an uncertain but appreciable margin relative to the equiatomic quinary).
fields.baseline: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi processed under the same thermomechanical conditions, which shows limited, rare hcp formation.
fields.boundary: The alloy must remain single-phase FCC after processing; the Mn reduction should not induce secondary phases; and the effect is most pronounced under high plastic deformation (strain >50%) and at cryogenic or ambient temperatures.
fields.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in strength and work hardening is not predetermined; effects may depend on the exact Mn concentration and local chemical ordering.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi (baseline) and one with reduced Mn while keeping a single-phase FCC structure. Subject both sets to identical thermomechanical processing and deformation (e.g. tensile testing to high true strain along with cryogenic and room temperature tests). Post-deformation, perform high-resolution TEM/HAADF-STEM to quantify the volume fraction and distribution of hcp laths.
measurements: Mechanical properties (yield strength, work hardening rate, ductility)
Quantitative TEM analysis of hcp/nanotwin areas
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mn-reduced alloy does not show statistically significant (as compared with experimental error) increases in both hcp phase fraction and mechanical strength/work hardening compared to the equiatomic baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C2
pool.builds_on: The paper’s findings that the thermally driven fcc-to-hcp transformation in CrCoNi is favored at low temperatures, while magnetic frustration in CrMnFeCoNi suppresses this mechanism (PMC5893566::web::000, PMC5893566::web::010).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis tests the role of deformation temperature as a variable to trigger differences in phase transformation behavior among alloys with varying constituent counts; it provides a controlled comparison across ternary, quaternary, and quinary systems under identical cryogenic deformation conditions—something not investigated in the original paper.

fields.hypothesis: Altering deformation temperature to more cryogenic conditions will preferentially enhance the localized fcc-to-hcp transformation in ternary and quaternary alloys relative to the quinary CrMnFeCoNi alloy, due to differences in thermal activation barriers and stacking fault energies.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic single-phase FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloys, including the quinary, quaternary, and ternary subsets after standard thermomechanical processing.
fields.intervention: Perform deformation tests (e.g., tensile or high-strain compression) at controlled cryogenic temperatures (lower than room temperature) for a controlled set of equiatomic alloys representing the CrCoNi ternary, one or more quaternary, and the CrMnFeCoNi quinary baseline.
fields.conditions: Identical thermomechanical processing and deformation conditions across all alloy variants, with the only variable being testing temperature (cryogenic, e.g., near liquid nitrogen temperature), ensuring that all specimens remain single-phase FCC prior to deformation.
fields.structural_mediator: Enhanced nucleation of nano-hcp laths at defect sites (stacking faults and twin boundaries) in alloys with fewer elements (ternary and selected quaternary) compared to the quinary alloy.
fields.mechanism: At cryogenic temperatures, thermal activation is reduced and the relative energy differences between fcc and hcp phases become more critical. In alloys such as CrCoNi, where the intrinsic stacking fault energy is low and magnetic effects favor an hcp transformation, the lowered temperature assists in overcoming the energy barrier for transformation at defects. In contrast, the magnetic frustration present in the quinary CrMnFeCoNi maintains a higher effective barrier. This temperature sensitivity results in measurable differences in phase transformation activity during deformation and, consequently, in the mechanical performance.
fields.predicted_outcome: Under cryogenic deformation, the CrCoNi ternary and certain quaternary alloys will exhibit a notably higher density of localized hcp structures and improved strain hardening compared to the quinary alloy, which will show suppressed hcp formation; the result is a relative increase in strength and ductility in the alloys where the transformation is more activated.
fields.baseline: Mechanical properties and microstructural evolution of equiatomic alloys deformed at room temperature, where differences are less pronounced.
fields.boundary: All alloys must remain single-phase FCC before deformation; testing at cryogenic temperatures must not induce extraneous phase instabilities; and the comparison is limited to high-strain deformation where transformation mechanisms are active.
fields.uncertainty: The precise quantitative enhancement in hcp formation and related strengthening in the ternary/quaternary alloys versus quinary is not exactly predictable; sensitivity to temperature may vary with slight compositional differences.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of equiatomic CrCoNi (ternary), a representative quaternary derivative, and CrMnFeCoNi (quinary). Deform all samples under identical strain and strain rate conditions at cryogenic temperatures (e.g., using a cryogenic tensile test rig). Post-deformation, conduct detailed TEM/HAADF-STEM analysis to quantify the hcp phase fraction and correlate with mechanical properties measured via stress–strain curves.
measurements: Yield strength and work hardening rate at cryogenic temperatures
Density and distribution of hcp laths via TEM characterization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryogenically deformed ternary and quaternary alloys do not show a statistically significant increase in hcp phase formation or improved mechanical properties relative to the quinary alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C3
pool.builds_on: The paper’s findings that dislocation activity is a key mechanism in energy absorption under high-speed deformation (PMC9374344::web::017) and that atomic bonding strength governs dislocation kinetics.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a novel thermomechanical processing step—controlled aging—to form nano-precipitates that further refine dislocation interactions, a strategy not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: A controlled aging (post–thermomechanical) heat treatment in the quinary (Cr‐Mn‐Fe‐Co‐Ni) alloy can induce nano‐scale, coherent precipitates that interact with dislocations, thereby enhancing strain hardening and ballistic resistance beyond the effect of Mn alone.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy processed into a single-phase FCC structure by standard thermomechanical treatments.
fields.intervention: Introduce a controlled aging heat treatment (e.g., holding at 500–600 °C for a short period followed by rapid quenching) to promote the formation of fine, coherent Cr-rich (or similar) nanoprecipitates without disrupting the FCC phase.
fields.conditions: Aging must be performed so as to maintain a single-phase FCC structure, with subsequent mechanical testing conducted at room temperature under high strain rate (ballistic-relevant) deformation.
fields.structural_mediator: Nano-scale precipitates acting as dislocation pinning sites that modify dislocation mobility, leading to a more continuous strain hardening response.
fields.mechanism: While the paper shows that Mn weakens overall metallic bonding and promotes early dislocation tangling, the introduction of finely dispersed precipitates provides additional barriers to dislocation motion. These precipitates force dislocations to bow and interact over longer distances, which enhances strain hardening and energy absorption during high-speed deformation. This mechanism builds on the observation of dislocation‐mediated plasticity (PMC9374344::web::017) but adds a new thermomechanical processing step to refine dislocation interactions.
fields.predicted_outcome: The aged quinary alloy should exhibit a higher strain hardening rate and ultimate tensile strength, as well as improved ballistic resistance (e.g., reduced penetration depth) compared with the as-processed baseline. Expected improvements in toughness might be in the 10–20% range, although the precise magnitude is uncertain.
fields.baseline: As-processed equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy with single-phase FCC microstructure.
fields.boundary: The benefits are expected only if the aging treatment yields stable, extremely fine (<10–20 nm) precipitates. Excessive coarsening or secondary phase formation would negate the benefits. Also, the improvement is most applicable at room temperature and high strain rates.
fields.uncertainty: Determining the optimal aging temperature and time to achieve the desired nano-precipitate size and distribution requires experimental calibration, and the precise quantitative advantage is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy samples: one following standard processing and the other with the additional controlled aging heat treatment. Conduct high strain rate tensile and ballistic impact tests. Use high-resolution TEM to verify nanoprecipitate formation and measure dislocation arrangements.
measurements: Strain hardening rate
Ultimate tensile strength
Ballistic penetration depth
Nanoprecipitate size and distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not show statistically significant improvements in strain hardening, strength, and ballistic resistance (accompanied by evidence of nanoscale precipitates) compared to the as-processed samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C4
pool.builds_on: The paper’s findings on the role of local deformation mechanisms (partial slip and stacking fault interactions) extended by proposing that even subtle short-range order in a nominally random alloy can modify these mechanisms.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the possibility that transient local chemical ordering, undetectable by average methods, can create a heterogeneous SFE landscape that modulates dislocation behavior and strain hardening, a concept not addressed in the original paper.

fields.hypothesis: Even though the as-processed Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy is nominally a random solid solution, slight short-range order (SRO) or local fluctuations in solute distribution can develop during thermomechanical processing and early stages of deformation. These localized regions, not obvious in average structural characterization, may lower the local stacking fault energy (SFE) and temporarily act as barriers to Shockley partial motion. This heterogeneous local SFE distribution would create more frequent interruptions during dislocation flow and promote the formation of stacking-fault parallelepipeds, enhancing strain hardening compared to the quaternary and ternary subsets.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic single-phase FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy and its equiatomic quaternary/ternary subsets produced by the same arc-melting, forging, rolling, and recrystallization processes yielding ~6 μm equiaxed grains.
fields.intervention: Use a post-deformation heat or short anneal treatment (or in situ annealing during deformation) designed to reveal and possibly enhance local short-range order, combined with advanced atom probe tomography (APT) and high-resolution STEM analysis to detect subtle solute fluctuations.
fields.conditions: Room-temperature quasi-static tensile tests under identical strain rate and imaging conditions (via in situ TEM), with complementary APT and STEM-EELS mapping before and after a mild anneal.
fields.structural_mediator: Transient regions of SRO or solute-rich clusters that locally reduce SFE.
fields.mechanism: Although the overall chemistry is random, minor atomic-scale segregation may occur. In regions where SRO develops, the local SFE is lower, enabling easier nucleation of Shockley partials but also causing their abrupt arrest at adjacent regions with higher local SFE. This intermittent dislocation motion leads to increased stacking fault density and promotes the formation of stacking-fault parallelepipeds, which enhance strain hardening and delay crack propagation. The quaternary and ternary alloys, with fewer element types, are less likely to develop such SRO fluctuations, resulting in more uniform SFE and smoother dislocation glide.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the quinary baseline, alloys in which local SRO is detected will show a higher density of stacking faults and stacking-fault parallelepipeds as observed in in situ TEM. The stress–strain curve should exhibit increased strain hardening in the quinary alloy. The effect size is expected to be moderate but statistically significant, though its precise magnitude is uncertain due to detection limits.
fields.baseline: The paper’s demonstration of Shockley partial mediated deformation and stacking-fault parallelepiped formation in CrMnFeCoNi (PMC4682111::web::005 and PMC4682111::web::013).
fields.boundary: This mechanism applies under room-temperature, quasi-static loading in thin-foil geometries where subtle SRO can affect local SFE; extreme temperatures or high strain rates may mask these effects.
fields.uncertainty: It is not yet quantitatively established how large the local SFE variations are due solely to SRO in these alloys; further atomistic measurements and modeling are needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys using identical protocols. Subject specimens to a mild post-deformation anneal to magnify any local SRO effects. Perform high-resolution APT and STEM-EELS mapping to detect solute fluctuations. Simultaneously, conduct in situ TEM tensile tests to quantify stacking fault and parallelepiped density in each alloy.
measurements: Quantitative APT data showing the presence (or absence) of solute clustering/SRO
STEM-EELS mapping of lattice SFE proxies
Density and spatial distribution of stacking faults and stacking-fault parallelepipeds from TEM images
Comparison of stress–strain curves focusing on strain hardening rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the quinary alloy does not exhibit any statistically significant short-range order or local SFE heterogeneity—and if the stacking fault density and strain hardening rates are similar to those in quaternary and ternary alloys—the hypothesis is refuted.

pool.label: C5
pool.builds_on: The paper’s documentation of extrinsic toughening through crack bridging via nanovoids and twinning (PMC4682111::web::010), extended by linking these observations to the influence of complex local bonding environments in multi-component alloys.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes that the intrinsic chemical complexity increases local stress heterogeneity that promotes nanovoid nucleation and subsequent twin-mediated crack bridging, rather than relying on precipitate formation, offering a new mechanistic angle not explored in the original study.

fields.hypothesis: The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy exhibits an enhanced propensity for nanovoid nucleation during deformation because of its complex local bonding environments. These nanovoids serve as precursors for developing nanoscale crack-bridging ligaments that subsequently undergo deformation twinning. In contrast, the simplified chemistry of quaternary and ternary alloys leads to more uniform bonding and lower local stress concentrations, reducing void nucleation frequency and the formation of effective extrinsic toughening bridges.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic single-phase FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy and its equiatomic quaternary/ternary subsets, produced via identical thermomechanical processing to achieve comparable grain sizes and phase purity.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled tensile deformation protocol emphasizing the late stages of plastic deformation and use high-resolution in situ TEM to monitor nanovoid nucleation and evolution near crack tips.
fields.conditions: Room-temperature quasi-static tensile testing with in situ TEM imaging focusing on the crack-tip region, where nanovoids and subsequent fiber-like bridging are observed.
fields.structural_mediator: Nanovoids that form from intersecting slip systems and thereafter evolve into nanoscale ligaments that undergo deformation twinning.
fields.mechanism: In the quinary alloy, the complexity of the local atomic bonding, due to the presence of five distinct species, may lead to statistically higher local stress concentrations under deformation. These stress concentrations can trigger nucleation of nanovoids along intersecting {111} slip planes. As deformation progresses, these voids coalesce into nanoscale bridges that, when subjected to further strain, deform by twinning and act to shield the crack tip. In alloys with fewer constituent elements, the atomic bonding is more uniform, resulting in fewer nucleation sites for voids, less coalescence into effective bridging structures, and thus a lower contribution from extrinsic toughening.
fields.predicted_outcome: Under identical deformation conditions, the quinary alloy will show a higher density of nanovoids in the semi-cohesive crack-tip zone, leading to more numerous and effective nanoscale bridges that exhibit deformation twinning, compared to the quaternary and ternary alloys. This should manifest as a measurable improvement in fracture toughness. The magnitude of improvement is expected to be moderate, though precise quantification is uncertain.

fields.boundary: This mechanism applies to specimens deformed under conditions where void nucleation from intersecting slip systems is active (late-stage deformation, room temperature) and where the microstructural scale is such that nanoscale bridging is observable. fields.uncertainty: The quantitative influence of local bonding variations on void nucleation frequency is not fully established, and its effect on extrinsic toughening may be sensitive to subtle processing differences.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys following identical processing routes. Formation and evolution of bridge-like ligaments including twin boundaries
Fracture toughness (KJIc) measured in subsequent mechanical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the quinary alloy does not show a statistically higher density of nanovoids and corresponding nanoscale bridges—and if the associated fracture toughness does not exceed that of the quaternary and ternary alloys—the hypothesis is falsified.

fields.boundary: Results are applicable under low temperature tensile deformation in single-phase FCC alloys with similar grain sizes and controlled GB characters.
fields.uncertainty: While the qualitative trends are supported, the exact quantitative impact of SFE variations on yield stress and twin density remains uncertain due to complex multi-element interactions.

Density and evolution of nanotwins/stacking faults
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured SFE does not correlate with the predicted changes in deformation mechanism (i.e., if lower SFE does not correspond to increased twinning and lower yield stress relative to higher SFE alloys), the hypothesis is falsified.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce a series of equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys with identical grain sizes and phases. Subject them to identical tensile deformation while performing post-mortem TEM and EBSD/KAM analyses to quantify dislocation densities and substructure evolution. Correlate these findings with measured yield strengths and work-hardening rates.
measurements: Dislocation density and substructure features (TEM, EBSD KAM)
Yield strength and strain-hardening curves from tensile tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant differences in retained dislocation densities or substructure features are observed between the alloys, or if these do not correlate with differences in work hardening and strength, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C15
pool.builds_on: The paper’s detailed analysis of dislocation dissociation and stacking fault energy in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA, highlighting the role of SFE in controlling dislocation behavior.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes that compositional reduction from quinary to lower-component alloys systematically alters the SFE, thereby modifying the operative dislocation mechanisms (cross-slip vs. twinning) and strain-hardening behavior—a factor not isolated in the paper, which focused mainly on bulk CRSS and size effects.

fields.hypothesis: Variations in stacking fault energy (SFE) induced by differing elemental interactions in the quinary versus the quaternary and ternary alloys alter the dislocation dissociation and cross-slip behavior, thereby affecting the strain-hardening behavior and failure modes.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni (quinary) alloy and its corresponding quaternary/ternary subsets, all in a single-phase FCC state after controlled thermomechanical processing.
fields.intervention: Synthesize compositions with one or more elements systematically removed (to form quaternary and ternary subsets) while ensuring identical processing; measure their stacking fault energies (via TEM analysis of Shockley partial separation) and perform mechanical deformation tests (micropillar compression or low-temperature deformation tests).
fields.conditions: Experiments conducted at room temperature and at cryogenic temperatures (e.g., 77 K) to probe temperature-dependent changes in SFE-related deformation mechanisms.
fields.structural_mediator: The dissociation width of dislocations (i.e., separation between Shockley partials) and the ease of cross-slip as mediated by the effective SFE.
fields.mechanism: In the quinary alloy, the complex interplay of elemental interactions results in an SFE (measured ~30 ± 5 mJ/m²) that controls the extent of dissociation of dislocations into partials. Removing one or more elements (forming quaternary/ternary alloys) alters the balance of atomic interactions and may lead to a shift in the SFE. A lower SFE will further increase the partial separation, inhibiting cross-slip and potentially promoting deformation twinning, while a higher SFE will facilitate cross-slip and alter strain hardening behavior. This variation in SFE, even if modest, changes the operative deformation mechanisms and thus the macroscopic mechanical properties.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to the quinary alloy, a quaternary or ternary alloy with a reduced SFE would be expected to show larger partial dislocation separations, reduced cross-slip, enhanced planar slip or even increased twinning activity, resulting in higher strain-hardening rates and possibly different failure modes (such as earlier onset of twinning-induced plasticity). Conversely, if the alloy’s SFE increases upon reducing constituent count, easier cross-slip may lower yield strength. Mechanical test data (stress-strain curves) and TEM measurement of partial separation distances should reveal these trends.
fields.baseline: The quinary alloy baseline as given in the paper [PMC5075899::web::abstract, discussion] with an SFE ~30 ± 5 mJ/m² and known dislocation dissociation behavior.
fields.boundary: Hypothesis is applicable only when all alloys remain single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing and are tested under comparable conditions.
fields.uncertainty: The magnitude of SFE change due to compositional variation may be modest, and the quantitative linking of SFE shifts to macroscopic mechanical properties requires careful interpretation; exact values might have higher uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys with the same thermomechanical history. Use TEM to measure Shockley partial separation distances (as a proxy for SFE) and measure macroscopic deformation behavior using micropillar compression or bulk tests at room and cryogenic temperatures. Compare strain-hardening rates and twinning activity.
measurements: Shockley partial separation distances
Stacking fault energy estimates derived from these distances
Stress-strain curves, yield strengths and strain-hardening rates
Observation of twinning or cross-slip in TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured SFE (or partial separation) remains unchanged across alloys and the mechanical behavior (e.g., strain hardening, twinning) does not vary in a manner predicted by SFE trends, then the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C14
top3.builds_on: the paper’s observation that non-recrystallized grains with retained dislocation/twin structures lead to higher yield strength, extending it to a role for dislocation substructure evolution controlled by compositional complexity.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the idea that increased compositional complexity in the quinary alloy retards dynamic recovery, preserving a denser dislocation network that synergistically interacts with twins to enhance mechanical properties—a factor not discussed in the original paper.

fields.hypothesis: Differential evolution of dislocation substructures during deformation arising from compositional complexity leads to enhanced preservation of dislocation networks in the quinary alloy, thereby increasing work hardening and delaying failure relative to the quaternary and ternary alloys.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic FCC alloys (quinary, quaternary, and ternary) produced by identical thermomechanical processing to yield similar grain sizes and initial recovery/twin states.
fields.intervention: Characterize dislocation density and substructure evolution in each alloy using high-resolution electron backscatter diffraction (KAM mapping) and TEM before and after controlled deformation protocols.
fields.conditions: Perform identical tensile tests at room and cryogenic temperatures while monitoring in situ or post-deformation substructure evolution, ensuring identical strain rates and deformation paths.
fields.structural_mediator: Persistent dislocation networks and subgrain structures that interact with deformation twins to enhance strain hardening.
fields.mechanism: The increased elemental complexity in the quinary alloy creates a more rugged energy landscape for dislocation motion and recovery, hindering dynamic annihilation and rearrangement of dislocations during deformation. This leads to higher retained dislocation densities and more robust dislocation-twin interactions that bolster strain hardening and yield strength. Conversely, the quaternary and ternary alloys, with fewer elements, allow more rapid dynamic recovery, resulting in smoother dislocation flow and lower work hardening.
fields.predicted_outcome: The quinary alloy should maintain a higher dislocation density (as measured by elevated KAM values and TEM-observed dislocation networks) after equivalent deformation, correlating with higher yield strength and strain hardening rates. The quaternary and ternary alloys will show a reduction in dislocation density (more dynamic recovery) and consequently lower mechanical strength by a measurable margin.
fields.baseline: The enhanced yield strength and strain hardening in the quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy documented in PMC5494191.
fields.boundary: All samples must have identical processing conditions, grain sizes, and phase composition; differences are attributed solely to compositional complexity affecting dislocation dynamics.
fields.uncertainty: While the concept of dynamic recovery differences is supported in alloys, precise quantification of its impact in these specific high-entropy system subsets remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce a series of equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys with identical grain sizes and phases. Subject them to identical tensile deformation while performing post-mortem TEM and EBSD/KAM analyses to quantify dislocation densities and substructure evolution. Correlate these findings with measured yield strengths and work-hardening rates.
measurements: Dislocation density and substructure features (TEM, EBSD KAM)
Yield strength and strain-hardening curves from tensile tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant differences in retained dislocation densities or substructure features are observed between the alloys, or if these do not correlate with differences in work hardening and strength, then the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C2
top3.builds_on: The paper’s findings that the thermally driven fcc-to-hcp transformation in CrCoNi is favored at low temperatures, while magnetic frustration in CrMnFeCoNi suppresses this mechanism (PMC5893566::web::000, PMC5893566::web::010).
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis tests the role of deformation temperature as a variable to trigger differences in phase transformation behavior among alloys with varying constituent counts; it provides a controlled comparison across ternary, quaternary, and quinary systems under identical cryogenic deformation conditions—something not investigated in the original paper.

fields.hypothesis: Altering deformation temperature to more cryogenic conditions will preferentially enhance the localized fcc-to-hcp transformation in ternary and quaternary alloys relative to the quinary CrMnFeCoNi alloy, due to differences in thermal activation barriers and stacking fault energies.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic single-phase FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloys, including the quinary, quaternary, and ternary subsets after standard thermomechanical processing.
fields.intervention: Perform deformation tests (e.g., tensile or high-strain compression) at controlled cryogenic temperatures (lower than room temperature) for a controlled set of equiatomic alloys representing the CrCoNi ternary, one or more quaternary, and the CrMnFeCoNi quinary baseline.
fields.conditions: Identical thermomechanical processing and deformation conditions across all alloy variants, with the only variable being testing temperature (cryogenic, e.g., near liquid nitrogen temperature), ensuring that all specimens remain single-phase FCC prior to deformation.
fields.structural_mediator: Enhanced nucleation of nano-hcp laths at defect sites (stacking faults and twin boundaries) in alloys with fewer elements (ternary and selected quaternary) compared to the quinary alloy.
fields.mechanism: At cryogenic temperatures, thermal activation is reduced and the relative energy differences between fcc and hcp phases become more critical. In alloys such as CrCoNi, where the intrinsic stacking fault energy is low and magnetic effects favor an hcp transformation, the lowered temperature assists in overcoming the energy barrier for transformation at defects. In contrast, the magnetic frustration present in the quinary CrMnFeCoNi maintains a higher effective barrier. This temperature sensitivity results in measurable differences in phase transformation activity during deformation and, consequently, in the mechanical performance.
fields.predicted_outcome: Under cryogenic deformation, the CrCoNi ternary and certain quaternary alloys will exhibit a notably higher density of localized hcp structures and improved strain hardening compared to the quinary alloy, which will show suppressed hcp formation; the result is a relative increase in strength and ductility in the alloys where the transformation is more activated.
fields.baseline: Mechanical properties and microstructural evolution of equiatomic alloys deformed at room temperature, where differences are less pronounced.
fields.boundary: All alloys must remain single-phase FCC before deformation; testing at cryogenic temperatures must not induce extraneous phase instabilities; and the comparison is limited to high-strain deformation where transformation mechanisms are active.
fields.uncertainty: The precise quantitative enhancement in hcp formation and related strengthening in the ternary/quaternary alloys versus quinary is not exactly predictable; sensitivity to temperature may vary with slight compositional differences.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of equiatomic CrCoNi (ternary), a representative quaternary derivative, and CrMnFeCoNi (quinary). Deform all samples under identical strain and strain rate conditions at cryogenic temperatures (e.g., using a cryogenic tensile test rig). Post-deformation, conduct detailed TEM/HAADF-STEM analysis to quantify the hcp phase fraction and correlate with mechanical properties measured via stress–strain curves.
measurements: Yield strength and work hardening rate at cryogenic temperatures
Density and distribution of hcp laths via TEM characterization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryogenically deformed ternary and quaternary alloys do not show a statistically significant increase in hcp phase formation or improved mechanical properties relative to the quinary alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C11
top3.builds_on: The paper’s mechanism linking high defect densities (stacking faults, twins) to amorphization during extreme deformation.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis incorporates the role of chemical short-range order in modulating local stacking fault energies—a factor beyond mere constituent count—to explain the observed differences in deformation behavior among these alloys.

fields.hypothesis: Variations in chemical short‐range order (CSRO) induced by complete versus reduced elemental complexity modulate the local stacking‐fault energy distribution, thereby altering defect accumulation and the onset of amorphization during deformation.
fields.material_initial_state: Thermomechanically processed, single‐phase FCC equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni (quinary) alloy and its equiatomic quaternary/ternary subsets with similar grain size and defect density pre-deformation.
fields.intervention: Perform controlled quasi‐static deformation tests while using atom probe tomography (APT) and high-resolution TEM to measure CSRO and local stacking-fault configurations at regions of deformation-induced defects.
fields.conditions: Experiments at ambient temperature with identical pre-deformation histories and strain rates ensuring similar macroscopic deformation conditions.
fields.structural_mediator: Localized regions with distinct chemical short-range order that affect the local stacking-fault energy and defect accumulation.
fields.mechanism: The full quinary alloy, due to the presence of all five elements, develops a more uniform and possibly stronger CSRO, which broadens the distribution of local stacking fault energies. This variation increases the free-energy barrier needed for defect coalescence into amorphous zones. In contrast, removal of one or two constituents in quaternary/ternary alloys reduces CSRO complexity, leading to a narrower stacking-fault energy distribution and lowering the effective barrier to amorphous region nucleation. This shift in microstructural evolution leads to differences in work hardening and failure behavior.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary/ternary alloys will exhibit earlier onset of amorphous island formation and a higher volumetric fraction of amorphous regions at the same strain—potentially a shift by tens of percent in the strain at which amorphization becomes noticeable. This should correlate with a less gradual work-hardening curve.
fields.baseline: The mechanical behavior and defect accumulation pathways observed in the fully equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy as documented in PMC7846165.
fields.boundary: Applies under quasi-static deformation at ambient temperature in single-phase FCC alloys with similar grain structures and pre-deformation defect densities.
fields.uncertainty: Quantitative relationship between CSRO variation and local stacking fault energy distribution is not well established prior to testing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare quinary, quaternary, and ternary specimens with identical thermomechanical processing. Apply identical quasi-static deformation protocols. Use APT and high-resolution TEM to map CSRO and measure the local stacking fault characteristics as deformation progresses. Simultaneously, record stress–strain responses.
measurements: Onset strain for amorphous region formation via TEM imaging
Distribution of local stacking fault energies inferred from defect configurations
Degree and scale of CSRO via atom probe tomography
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If quaternary/ternary alloys do not show a systematically lower onset strain for amorphous formation or if differences in CSRO and local stacking fault energy distributions are not observed between the full quinary and reduced alloys, the hypothesis is refuted.
